items.prompt: How many tones does standard Vietnamese have, counting the level (unmarked) tone?

options.label: Eight
Six
Four
Five

rubric: Vietnamese has six tones including the level tone.
Four is the Mandarin count; five is a common miscount that omits the level tone.

items.prompt: Which word means 'hello' in Vietnamese?

options.label: Tạm biệt
Xin chào
Xin lỗi
Cảm ơn

rubric: Xin chào is the standard greeting.
The others mean thank you, goodbye and sorry.

items.prompt: Which Vietnamese word means 'thank you'?

options.label: Xin chào
Không
Cảm ơn
Xin lỗi

rubric: Cảm ơn means thank you.
Xin lỗi is 'sorry' and không is 'no/not'.

items.prompt: What does the number 'ba' mean in Vietnamese counting?

options.label: Four
Two
Three
Five

rubric: Ba is three (một, hai, ba).
Learners often mix it up with hai (two) or bốn (four).

items.prompt: Which writing system does modern Vietnamese use?

options.label: Latin alphabet with added diacritics
Thai-style abugida with inherent vowels
Chinese characters used for every word
Arabic script with added dots and marks

rubric: Quốc ngữ is Latin-based with diacritics.
Chinese characters were historically used but are not the modern script.

items.prompt: Which of the following are Vietnamese words for family members? Select all that apply.

options.label: nhà (house)
mẹ (mother)
sách (book)
bố (father)

rubric: Mẹ and bố are mother and father.
Nhà and sách are house and book, not family terms.

items.prompt: You are visiting Hanoi and a shopkeeper greets you. You want to politely say 'thank you' after buying a bottle of water and then leave. Which word do you say for 'thank you'?

options.label: Không có gì
Xin lỗi
Cảm ơn
Xin chào

rubric: Cảm ơn is thank you.
Không có gì means 'you're welcome', and xin lỗi means sorry.

items.prompt: Why does the difference between 'ma', 'má' and 'mả' matter in Vietnamese?

options.label: Accents only show where to stress the word
Tone marks change the meaning of the word
They are just regional spelling variants
Marks only show the word is a loanword

rubric: Tone marks are part of the word and change its meaning.
Treating marks as stress or optional spelling is a common English-speaker error.

items.prompt: What is the basic word order of a simple Vietnamese sentence like 'Tôi ăn cơm' (I eat rice)?

options.label: Object, subject, verb
Subject, object, verb
Verb, subject, object
Subject, verb, object

rubric: Vietnamese is SVO.
Subject-object-verb is the pattern of Japanese or Korean.

items.prompt: How does Vietnamese usually show that an action happened in the past, as in 'Tôi đã ăn' (I ate)?

options.label: A marker word like 'đã' goes before an unchanged verb
A different tone mark is put on the pronoun, so 'tôi' changes
The verb takes a past ending, much as English adds -ed
A classifier like 'cái' or 'con' is placed before the verb

rubric: Vietnamese verbs do not conjugate; markers like đã show time.
Changing verb endings is an English or European habit.

items.prompt: In 'Tôi không ăn thịt' (I do not eat meat), what is the function of 'không'?

options.label: It means 'very', intensifying the verb after it
It marks the past tense of the verb after it
It turns the sentence into a yes/no question
It negates the verb that follows

rubric: Không placed before a verb negates it.
Question and tense markers are other words, such as không at sentence end or đã.

items.prompt: In 'hai quyển sách' (two books), what role does 'quyển' play?

options.label: A classifier between the number and the noun
A plural ending attached to the noun, like English -s
A verb meaning 'to have', placed after the number
A particle meaning 'of', linking number and noun

rubric: Quyển is a classifier used when counting books.
Vietnamese nouns do not take plural endings.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe Vietnamese writing and sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Diacritics on vowels can show tone
Every written syllable carries a visible tone mark
Verbs change their endings to show the person
Syllables are written as separate words with spaces between them

rubric: Syllables are space-separated, and diacritics mark tone.
Verbs do not conjugate, and the level tone has no mark, so the last option is tricky but marks are not on every syllable.

items.prompt: A learner says 'Tôi là giáo viên' to a new classmate, then adds 'Bạn là giáo viên không?' with không at the end. The classmate answers with 'Không, tôi là sinh viên.' What did the learner's second sentence do?

options.label: Said that the learner is also a student, like the classmate
Stated that the classmate is not a teacher, using không
Asked where the classmate works, using a question word
Asked a yes/no question with final không

rubric: Sentence-final không forms a yes/no question.
Reading it as a negative statement confuses it with preverbal không.

items.prompt: Which of these words carries the falling (huyền) tone?

options.label: mả
má
mà
mã

rubric: The grave accent (`) marks the huyền tone, so 'mà' is correct.
'má' is the rising sắc tone, 'mả' the dipping hỏi tone and 'mã' the creaky ngã tone, which learners often confuse.

items.prompt: Which noun normally takes the classifier 'con'?

options.label: chó (dog)
sách (book)
nhà (house)
bàn (table)

rubric: 'Con' is the classifier for animals, so 'con chó' is correct.
Books, tables and houses use other classifiers (quyển, cái, căn), and learners often over-generalise 'con'.

items.prompt: How does a Vietnamese adjective normally sit relative to the noun it describes?

options.label: Before the noun, as in 'lớn nhà' (big house)
After the noun, as in 'nhà lớn' (big house)
After the noun only when the noun is plural
Before the noun, as in 'đẹp hoa' (pretty flower)

rubric: Adjectives follow the noun, so 'nhà lớn' is right.
Distractors copy English order or invent a plural rule; Vietnamese nouns do not mark plural.

items.prompt: In 'Tôi đã ăn cơm', what does the word 'đã' tell you?

options.label: The action is happening right now
The action is about to happen soon
The sentence is a polite question
The action is already completed

rubric: 'Đã' is a past/completed marker placed before the verb.
'Sẽ' marks future and 'đang' marks ongoing action, which are the likely confusions.

items.prompt: Why is 'Anh ấy không phải là bác sĩ' the right way to say 'He is not a doctor'?

options.label: 'Không phải' is used only when asking questions about people
'Không' alone always negates nouns, and 'phải' only adds politeness
Negating an identity noun uses 'không phải là', not 'không' alone
'Phải' marks the past tense of the negation in this sentence

rubric: 'Là' sentences with nouns are negated with 'không phải là'.
Learners often transfer 'không' alone from verbs and adjectives to nouns.

items.prompt: Which of these are Vietnamese question words? Select all that apply.

options.label: ai (who)
gì (what)
và (and)
đâu (where)
nhưng (but)

rubric: Ai, đâu and gì are question words for who, where and what.
'Và' and 'nhưng' are conjunctions, not question words.

items.prompt: A learner texts a Vietnamese friend and writes 'ban' in every message, leaving off all diacritics because the keyboard is awkward. The friend replies that some messages are confusing. The learner meant 'bạn' (friend/you). What best explains the confusion?

options.label: Tone marks distinguish words, so dropping them can change or hide the meaning
The word 'bạn' needs a classifier before it, and that was missing
Vietnamese uses diacritics only on capital letters, so lower case was wrong
Diacritics are only decorative, and the friend is being too strict about spelling

rubric: In Vietnamese the tone and vowel marks are part of the spelling and separate words.
Distractors treat diacritics as optional or invent capitalisation and classifier rules.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I am eating rice' (action in progress)?

options.label: Tôi ăn đang cơm
Tôi đang ăn cơm
Đang tôi cơm ăn
Tôi cơm ăn đang

rubric: The pattern is subject + đang + verb + object.
The other options misplace the progressive marker or use the wrong word order.

items.prompt: How do you say the number 25 in Vietnamese?

options.label: mười hai lăm
hai lăm mươi
hai mươi lăm
hai năm mươi

rubric: Tens come first (hai mươi = 20), then the unit, and 5 becomes 'lăm' after a ten.
Other options scramble the tens and units order.

items.prompt: You pick up an item in a shop. Which sentence asks 'How much is this?'

options.label: Cái này của ai vậy?
Cái này là gì vậy?
Cái này ở đâu ra?
Cái này bao nhiêu?

rubric: 'Bao nhiêu tiền' asks for a price.
The distractors ask where, what and whose, and use similar frames.

items.prompt: Which phrase correctly says 'my book' using the possessive word của?

options.label: tôi sách của
sách tôi của
của tôi sách
sách của tôi

rubric: The possessed noun comes first, then 'của', then the owner.
Other options reverse the English-style order or misplace 'của'.

items.prompt: Which sentence says 'I haven't eaten yet'?

options.label: Tôi không ăn
Tôi sẽ ăn
Tôi đã ăn
Tôi chưa ăn

rubric: 'Chưa' means 'not yet' and is placed before the verb.
'Không ăn' means don't eat, 'đã ăn' means already ate, 'sẽ ăn' means will eat.

items.prompt: Which sentences correctly use 'là' (to be)? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cô ấy là giáo viên.
Tôi là sinh viên.
Nhà tôi là lớn.
Tôi là mệt.

rubric: 'Là' links a subject to a noun, as in 'student' and 'teacher'.
'Là' is not used before adjectives such as 'mệt' or 'lớn', a common English-influenced error.

items.prompt: You are in Hanoi and need the bathroom. An elderly woman, about grandmother age, is sitting nearby. You want to get her attention and ask politely where the bathroom is. Which sentence fits best?

options.label: Mày ơi, nhà vệ sinh ở đâu?
Cháu ơi, nhà vệ sinh ở đâu ạ?
Bà ơi, nhà vệ sinh ở đâu ạ?
Em ơi, nhà vệ sinh ở đâu ạ?

rubric: 'Bà' is the right address for an elderly woman, and 'ạ' adds politeness.
'Em' and 'cháu' address younger people, and 'mày' is rude.

items.prompt: You are writing a price in words on a receipt: 25 (in the tens-and-five pattern). Which form follows the standard rule for the digit 5 after a tens word?

options.label: hai mươi lăm
hai mươi năm
hai mươi lẻ năm
hai mươi nhăm lăm

rubric: After mươi, five is written lăm, so 25 is hai mươi lăm.
Hai mươi năm means twenty years, a common confusion with the word năm.

items.prompt: You are writing a shop sign listing items for sale. Which phrase correctly says 'three pens' (bút) and keeps the standard classifier for long thin objects?

options.label: ba con bút
ba quyển bút
ba cái bút
ba cây bút

rubric: Animals take the classifier con, so ba con mèo is correct.
Cái and quyển are classifiers for objects and books; mèo con means kitten.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly asks a yes/no question, 'Do you like coffee?'

options.label: Bạn có thích cà phê không?
Có bạn thích cà phê không?
Bạn có thích không cà phê?
Bạn thích có cà phê không?

rubric: The yes/no frame is có + verb phrase + không, wrapping the whole predicate.
The other options break the frame by misplacing có or không.

items.prompt: Write 'horse' on the syllable ma, pronounced with the broken rising ngã tone (~). Which form is it?

options.label: má
mạ
mã
mà

rubric: The ngã tone mark is the tilde, giving mã, which means horse.
Mà, má and mạ carry the huyền, sắc and nặng tones and mean other words.

items.prompt: Which phrase correctly says 'my friend's new book'?

options.label: bạn tôi của quyển sách mới
mới quyển sách của bạn tôi
quyển mới sách của bạn tôi
quyển sách mới của bạn tôi

rubric: Vietnamese puts the noun first, then the adjective, then của and the possessor.
The others copy English order or split the classifier from its noun.

items.prompt: Which sentences correctly use aspect or negation markers? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tôi chưa gặp anh ấy.
Tôi đi sẽ Hà Nội ngày mai.
Anh ấy không chưa ăn cơm.
Cô ấy đã học xong rồi.
Tôi sẽ đi Hà Nội ngày mai.

rubric: Sẽ, đã and chưa all stand before the verb or predicate.
Placing sẽ after the verb or stacking không with chưa is ungrammatical.

items.prompt: You are 25 and sit in a cafe in Hanoi. The waiter looks about five years older than you. You want to politely order one coffee and show appropriate kinship address. What do you say?

options.label: Anh ơi, cho anh một ly cà phê.
Anh ơi, cho em một ly cà phê.
Ông ơi, cho tôi một ly cà phê.
Em ơi, cho anh một ly cà phê.

rubric: You call an older man anh and refer to yourself as em.
The others reverse the roles, use anh for yourself, or use ông, which is for much older men.

items.prompt: A learner writes 'Tôi ăn cơm đang' meaning 'I am eating rice'. What is the underlying error?

options.label: Cơm is a countable noun, so it needs the classifier con before it.
Aspect markers like đang come before the main verb, not after the object.
Aspect markers like đang come after the object when the action is still ongoing.
Đang is only used with adjectives, so the verb ăn needs là before it.

rubric: Aspect markers such as đang, đã and sẽ precede the verb.
The distractors invent rules about object position or là.

items.prompt: A learner meaning 'grandmother' (bà) is heard by a listener as 'three' or 'father' (ba). What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The vowel was too long, which changes the word's meaning.
The final consonant was dropped, which merges the two words.
The learner used the wrong classifier before the noun.
The low falling huyền tone was missing, leaving a flat tone.

rubric: Bà and ba differ only in tone, so a flat tone loses the distinction.
Vowel length, final consonants and classifiers are not what separates these syllables.

items.prompt: Why is 'Cô ấy là đẹp' ungrammatical for 'She is beautiful'?

options.label: Đẹp must come before the pronoun in a descriptive sentence.
Adjectives act as predicates by themselves; là links two nouns.
Là requires the intensifier rất immediately before the adjective.
Là is only used for past states, so it clashes with the present.

rubric: Vietnamese adjectives work as verbs, so no copula is used before them.
Là joins nouns (Cô ấy là giáo viên); the other rules are invented.

items.prompt: A learner uses 'tôi' and 'bạn' when talking to an elderly neighbour, and it sounds cold. Which analysis explains this?

options.label: Elders are addressed by given name alone, so any pronoun at all sounds stiff and odd.
Kinship terms encode age and relationship, so neutral tôi and bạn sound distant to an elder.
Tôi and bạn belong to formal writing, so speech needs different pronouns with every listener.
Tôi and bạn imply a past tense, so they clash with the ongoing conversation with a neighbour.

rubric: Vietnamese address uses kinship terms like ông or bà to show respect and closeness.
Tôi and bạn are neutral or peer forms; the other claims about writing, tense or names are false.

items.prompt: A learner says 'Tôi không là giáo viên' to mean 'I am not a teacher'. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: The sentence should use chưa, because not being a teacher is temporary.
Negating là with a noun needs không phải là, not không alone.
Không cannot be used in any sentence containing a noun.
Giáo viên needs a classifier before it to be negated.

rubric: The negative of là is không phải là: Tôi không phải là giáo viên.
Chưa means not yet and does not fit; the other claims are invented.

items.prompt: Which pairs of syllables differ ONLY in tone, not in vowel or consonant? Select all that apply.

options.label: ma – má
mua – mưa
cá – cà
bàn – bạn
đi – đo

rubric: Ma/má, cá/cà and bàn/bạn share the same letters and differ in tone marks.
Mua/mưa and đi/đo differ in vowel, so they are not tone-only pairs.

items.prompt: At 8 pm your friend calls and asks 'Bạn đang làm gì đó?' You are in the middle of dinner and answer 'Tôi đã ăn cơm.' Your friend starts a long story, then is puzzled when you say you cannot talk now. Why did the misunderstanding happen?

options.label: Cơm is a noun that cannot take a tense marker, so the sentence was ungrammatical and unclear to your friend.
Đã marks the future, so your friend thought you would eat later and were free to talk now.
Đó at the end of the question means you should have answered with chưa to show you had not yet eaten.
Đã marks a completed action, so your friend thought you had finished; you needed đang.

rubric: Đang marks an action in progress and đã a completed one; your answer did not match the question.
The distractors misassign đã to the future or invent noun and đó rules.

items.prompt: A learner meant to say `cá` (fish) at a restaurant, but the server heard `cà` (eggplant). Which tone error best explains the mix-up?

options.label: Used a glottalised nặng tone instead of the high rising sắc tone
Used a level ngang tone instead of the high rising sắc tone
Used a dipping hỏi tone instead of the high rising sắc tone
Used a low falling huyền tone instead of the high rising sắc tone

rubric: The server heard `cà`, which carries the huyền (low falling) tone, so the learner produced huyền where sắc was needed.
The other options name real tones, but they would produce `cạ`, `cả` or `ca`, not `cà`.

items.prompt: A learner writes `Tôi đọc hai cuốn báo mỗi sáng` for 'I read two newspapers every morning'. A native speaker says it sounds off. What is the best analysis?

options.label: The number `hai` forces the general classifier `cái`, because quantities override nouns
Classifiers must come after the noun, so the order `báo hai cuốn` is required
Báo names a living thing, so it takes `con`, because classifiers track animacy
Báo is a flat printed sheet, so it takes `tờ`, while `cuốn` fits bound volumes

rubric: Newspapers are counted with `tờ`, a classifier for sheets, while `cuốn` suits bound books.
Distractors invent animacy or word-order rules that do not govern classifier choice.

items.prompt: A teacher marks `Hôm qua tôi đi chợ` wrong and demands `Hôm qua tôi đã đi chợ`. What is the best diagnosis of the correction?

options.label: The correction is right, because every Vietnamese past-time sentence needs `đã` to be grammatical
The correction is right, because `đi` has no tense unless a marker such as `đã` directly follows it
The correction is wrong, because `đã` is reserved for written Vietnamese and sounds odd in speech
The correction is wrong, because a time word like `hôm qua` already fixes the time, so `đã` is optional

rubric: Vietnamese verbs do not inflect, and tense markers like `đã` are optional when a time word makes the time clear.
Distractors treat `đã` as obligatory like an English past ending, or wrongly limit it to writing.

items.prompt: A 22-year-old learner chats with a friend's 55-year-old mother and calls her `bạn` while referring to themselves as `tôi`. Why does this come across as cold or odd?

options.label: `Bạn` is mainly a written-style word that is rarely said aloud, so using it in conversation makes the learner sound like a textbook
`Tôi` is a childish form that adults avoid in conversation, so it signals that the learner is not yet mature enough to talk to elders
Vietnamese discourages any pronoun when speaking to older women, so the learner should omit both words and use only the name
Kinship terms like `cô` or `bác` with `cháu` mark relative age and warmth, while `bạn`/`tôi` imply distant equals

rubric: Vietnamese pronouns encode relative age and relationship; `bạn`/`tôi` treat the elder as a peer or stranger.
Other options make up register rules about `bạn`, `tôi`, or pronoun omission.

items.prompt: A learner trained on a Hà Nội recording is puzzled that the speaker pronounces `da` (skin), `gia` (family) and `ra` (go out) identically. What explains this?

options.label: The recording used a faulty microphone that flattened the vowels so the initials blurred together
These three words are homophones in every dialect, so the spelling difference is only historical
Northern speakers drop the initial consonant entirely, leaving only the vowel and its tone
In the northern accent the initials `d`, `gi` and `r` have merged into the same /z/ sound

rubric: Northern Vietnamese merges `d`, `gi` and `r` into /z/, whereas southern speech often keeps them apart.
Distractors claim consonant dropping or universal homophony, which is false.

items.prompt: Which of these word pairs differ ONLY in tone, with identical consonants and vowels? Select all that apply.

options.label: `nam` and `năm`
`ba` and `bà`
`mua` and `mưa`
`cô` and `cố`

rubric: `ba`/`bà` and `cô`/`cố` differ only in tone marks.
`nam`/`năm` differ in the vowel (a vs ă) and `mua`/`mưa` in u vs ư, so the vowel changes.

items.prompt: A learner texts a friend without any diacritics: `Minh di cho nhe`. The friend replies asking whether they mean going to the market or something else, since `cho` could be `chợ`, `chó` or `cho`. Which statement best analyses the source of the confusion?

options.label: Without diacritics, distinct words share one spelling, so only context separates them
The particle `nhé` turns the statement into a question, so the friend cannot tell which answer is wanted
The friend cannot parse `di` as a verb of motion because the missing marks change its word class here
Quốc ngữ spelling is ambiguous even with diacritics, so the marks add little to meaning in writing

rubric: Tone marks and diacritics are part of the spelling; removing them merges words like `chợ`, `chó` and `cho`.
Distractors blame vocabulary, claim diacritics are useless, or misread the particle `nhé`.

items.prompt: A learner has two weeks in Hồ Chí Minh City and wants to be understood. Criteria: efficient use of limited practice time, and speech that southern listeners will follow. Southern speakers commonly merge hỏi and ngã. Which plan is best?

options.label: Drill the other four tone contrasts to accuracy, and learn hỏi/ngã mainly as spelling rather than a spoken contrast
Copy northern pronunciation of all six tones, since it is the standard and southerners will adjust easily
Skip tones entirely and rely on context, since southern listeners ignore pitch differences
Spend most sessions on hỏi versus ngã, since it is the hardest pair and must be perfect to be understood

rubric: Where hỏi and ngã merge in speech, time is better spent on contrasts listeners actually use.
Other options overinvest in a merged pair, ignore tones, or mismatch the target accent.

items.prompt: A student wants to tell a teacher they have not understood the lesson. Criteria: respectful, natural for a student, and warm in tone. Which sentence is best?

options.label: `Cô ơi, em chưa hiểu bài nhé.`
`Cô ơi, tôi chưa hiểu bài ạ.`
`Thưa cô, em chưa hiểu bài ạ.`
`Thưa cô, con chưa hiểu bài đâu ạ.`

rubric: `Em` for the student and `cô` for the teacher, with `thưa` and `ạ`, is respectful and natural.
The others use `tôi`/`bạn`, which sound distant, or the casual `nhé`, which lacks deference.

items.prompt: A learner who wants everyday conversation ranks which error to fix first. Criterion: which most often makes listeners fail to understand the intended word? Which should be fixed first?

options.label: Omitting `đã` before a verb when a time word like `hôm qua` already marks the past
Using the wrong tone on a content word, such as `cá` versus `cà`
Leaving out the classifier `con` before an animal noun, as in `chó` for `con chó`
Leaving out the polite particle `ạ` when answering someone clearly older than you

rubric: A wrong tone turns a word into a different word, so it breaks comprehension most.
The other errors are usually still understood, costing only naturalness or politeness.

items.prompt: A tutor claims, 'Vietnamese has almost no grammar because its words never change form.' Judged against how the language works, which critique is best?

options.label: The claim is correct, since without inflection the words in a sentence can be put in nearly any order and still keep their meaning
The claim is half right, since tones carry the grammatical information in place of endings and the rest of the language is vocabulary
The claim is flawed, since grammar is carried by word order, classifiers, particles and markers rather than inflection
The claim is flawed, since Vietnamese verbs do inflect for tense, though this is mostly seen in formal writing and in the south

rubric: Lack of inflection does not mean lack of grammar; meaning depends on order, classifiers and particles.
Distractors assume free word order, confuse tones with grammar, or invent inflection.

items.prompt: A learner wants the most natural, everyday way to ask a friend whether they have eaten yet, expecting that the meal may still be pending. Which is the best choice?

options.label: `Bạn đã ăn cơm hay không?`
`Bạn ăn cơm không?`
`Bạn có ăn cơm đâu?`
`Bạn ăn cơm chưa?`

rubric: `Chưa` at the end asks 'yet?' and fits a pending event.
`Không` asks a general yes/no about habit or willingness, and the others are unnatural or change the sense.

items.prompt: A beginner wants reading material for the next six months. Criteria: build lasting reading ability, tone accuracy and vocabulary for daily life. Which selection criteria are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Texts with matching audio, so spelling and tones are learned together
Texts without tone marks, because removing them lowers the load
Texts printed with full diacritics, because tone marks are part of the spelling
Texts of only literary classics, because older vocabulary is more prestigious and lasts

items.prompt: A learner in Hà Nội has a partner from Cần Thơ. Their textbook teaches `bố` for 'father' and `quả` for 'fruit', but the partner's family says `ba` and `trái`. Criteria: be understood in both settings, and avoid confusion. Which approach is best?

options.label: Switch fully to the family's forms, since textbook variants will never be heard again
Treat them as regional variants, choose one set to speak and learn the other for recognition
Use only the textbook forms, since the partner's family must be using incorrect Vietnamese
Mix both sets randomly in each sentence, since a listener will understand either one anyway

rubric: `Bố/ba` and `quả/trái` are accepted regional variants, so a consistent active set with passive recognition of the other is efficient.
Distractors call a dialect wrong, discard one variant, or mix them without consistency.

items.prompt: You are 25 and speak to a stranger woman who runs a shop and looks about 40 to 45, roughly your parent's younger sibling's age. You want a polite way to say 'you' that shows respect without implying she is elderly. Which term is the best choice?

options.label: bà, which marks grandmother age and would suggest she is elderly
em, which is used for someone younger than you or a child
cô, which fits a woman about a parent's younger sibling's age and is respectful
chị, which is used for a woman only slightly older than you, like an older sister

rubric: 'Cô' suits a woman roughly a parent's younger sibling's age and is respectful without suggesting old age.
'Bà' implies grandmother age, 'chị' fits someone only slightly older, and 'em' is for someone younger.

items.prompt: A colleague claims: 'In formal emails you can drop tone marks, since context disambiguates.' Which critique of this claim is strongest?

options.label: Tone marks record pronunciation only, so readers recover the intended word from consonants and vowels alone in formal text.
Context helps, but unmarked forms like 'ban' merge many different words, so formal text becomes ambiguous and looks careless.
Formal Vietnamese is read aloud with a flat tone, so a written tone mark adds no information that the reader needs at all.
Dropping is allowed only when a vowel already carries a circumflex or horn, because those marks fix the tone of the word.

rubric: Tone marks are part of the spelling and distinguish many words that look identical without them.
Distractors wrongly treat tones as speech-only or claim other diacritics replace tone marks.

items.prompt: A learner says 'đã' is simply the past-tense marker and must appear in every sentence about the past. Judge this claim against the sentence 'Ngày mai khi anh đến, tôi đã ăn xong rồi.'

options.label: The claim fails: đã actually marks the future, and sẽ is the word reserved for past events inside sentences with a time clause.
The claim fails: đã marks completion before a reference time, so it fits a future-oriented sentence and can be omitted when time is clear.
The claim holds: đã is the only way Vietnamese can show past time, so dropping it makes every past-time sentence ungrammatical.
The claim holds: đã here is an error, because the sentence refers to tomorrow and a past marker cannot occur with a future time word.

rubric: Đã marks completion relative to a reference point, not absolute past, and is often optional.
Distractors treat Vietnamese as having obligatory tense like English.

items.prompt: A learner will study mostly with a Southern Vietnamese tutor but wants to spell hỏi and ngã correctly. Which judgement about the study plan is soundest?

options.label: Ignore the difference, because hỏi and ngã are interchangeable in writing and a mismatch never changes which word is spelled.
Memorise the hỏi or ngã spelling with each word, since many Southern speakers pronounce both alike and speech will not reveal the mark.
Learn a rule from the initial consonant, since ngã occurs only after nasal initials and hỏi elsewhere, with no exceptions at all.
Rely on the tutor's pronunciation, since Southern speech marks ngã with a glottal break that keeps it clearly distinct from hỏi.

rubric: Southern speech commonly merges hỏi and ngã, so spelling must be learned per word.
Distractors assume the contrast is audible, irrelevant, or fully rule-governed.

items.prompt: In a meeting Linh turns to a colleague and says 'We should leave now', meaning herself and the colleague together. Judging by the criterion that the listener must be included, which rendering is best?

options.label: Chúng nó nên đi bây giờ.
Chúng tôi nên đi bây giờ.
Các bạn nên đi bây giờ.
Chúng ta nên đi bây giờ.

rubric: 'Chúng ta' is the inclusive 'we' covering the listener.
'Chúng tôi' excludes the listener, 'chúng nó' means 'they', and 'các bạn' means 'you all'.

items.prompt: A friend says 'Vietnamese has no grammar because words never change form.' Which responses are sound criticisms of this claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: Particles such as đã, đang and sẽ mark time and aspect without any inflection.
Word order carries roles: 'Mai yêu Nam' and 'Nam yêu Mai' differ in who loves whom.
Classifiers like con and cái combine with numbers and nouns by systematic rules.
Grammar exists only where suffixes mark case and gender, so the claim is true by definition.
Verbs conjugate for person through tone changes, which is the grammar in question.

rubric: Vietnamese expresses grammar through word order, particles and classifiers rather than inflection.
Distractors invent tonal conjugation or define grammar as inflection only.

items.prompt: A tutor corrects a learner's 'Cô ấy là đẹp' to 'Cô ấy đẹp'. The learner asks whether 'là' can go before any adjective for emphasis. The tutor must give the most accurate and generalisable reply. Which reply is best?

options.label: Là works like English 'to be', so it can precede adjectives, nouns and locations in standard Vietnamese, and the learner's sentence was just redundant.
Là is expected before adjectives in formal speech and is usually dropped in casual speech, so the learner's original sentence was merely too formal.
Adjectives act as predicates without là; là links a subject to a noun or identity, as in 'Cô ấy là giáo viên'.
Là is needed before adjectives when the subject is a pronoun such as ấy, while a noun subject such as 'cô giáo' lets the adjective follow directly.

rubric: Vietnamese adjectives are stative predicates and take no copula; là links noun phrases.
Distractors carry over English 'be' or invent register or pronoun rules.

items.prompt: You are writing a report in Vietnamese and want to say 'I got scolded by my boss' (an unwelcome event) while keeping the boss as the named agent. Which sentence is correct and carries that meaning?

options.label: Tôi bị sếp mắng.
Tôi được sếp mắng.
Tôi sếp bị mắng.
Tôi bị mắng sếp.

rubric: 'Bị' marks an adversative passive-like experience with the agent before the verb.
'Được' marks a beneficial event, and the other options break the word order.

items.prompt: A host you call 'cô' offers more food. Compose a reply that stays polite, calls yourself 'cháu', and declines because you are full. Which reply meets every constraint?

options.label: Dạ, em cảm ơn cô, em no rồi ạ.
Cảm ơn cô, tôi no rồi, cô đừng mời nữa.
Dạ, cháu cảm ơn cô, cháu no rồi ạ.
Cháu cảm ơn cô, cháu no rồi nhé, cô cứ ăn đi.

rubric: It keeps cô/cháu consistent and adds the respectful particles dạ and ạ.
The others use cold 'tôi', the wrong self-pronoun 'em', or casual 'nhé'.

items.prompt: You are writing a sentence meaning 'He is both smart and kind', presenting the two qualities as simultaneous and equal, with no sense that the second adds to the first. Which construction fits best?

options.label: Anh ấy vừa thông minh vừa tốt bụng.
Anh ấy không những thông minh mà còn tốt bụng.
Anh ấy vừa thông minh và vừa tốt bụng đấy.
Anh ấy thông minh vừa tốt bụng vừa.

items.prompt: Compose a sentence saying 'I have never eaten durian', meaning you have never had the experience. Which sentence fits?

options.label: Tôi chưa bao giờ ăn sầu riêng.
Tôi không bao giờ ăn sầu riêng.
Tôi chưa đã ăn sầu riêng bao giờ.
Tôi không chưa ăn sầu riêng.

rubric: 'Chưa bao giờ' expresses never so far, an experience not yet had.
'Không bao giờ' means habitually never, and the others are ungrammatical.

items.prompt: A beginner tone course uses only isolated words read slowly by one Northern speaker. The goal is to understand everyday speech from varied speakers. Which additions would fix the gaps? Select all that apply.

options.label: Only slower recordings, so that no tone is ever heard at natural conversational speed.
Recordings of several speakers, including Southern accents, so tone shapes are heard in varied voices.
Text with diacritics removed, so learners rely on pitch alone to identify every word.
Short connected phrases, so learners hear how tones behave in natural, faster speech.
Sentences with context cues, so learners use meaning to resolve tones they hear unclearly.

rubric: Variation in speakers, connected speech and context all build real comprehension.
Removing diacritics or avoiding natural speed works against the stated goal.
